Create a two-column list: left column — three causes discussed in class and a one-sentence explanation whether each is long-term or short-term; right column — one piece of evidence from the lesson text that supports each classification.

mentor_moment.story: A student I taught argued the Terror showed revolutionaries were united; after we reviewed arrest and execution numbers and internal disputes, she changed her view and said the evidence showed deep divisions.
mentor_moment.takeaway: Use specific evidence (numbers and named events) to test your first impression; facts can change which side of an argument you support.
mentor_moment.title: When evidence changes your side

anticipated_questions: Was the Bastille the start of the Revolution?
Did the Estates General meet for the first time in 1789?
What were the three estates exactly?
teacher_script.board_action: Write: "Quick recap: Storming of the Bastille; Estates General called (May 1789)."
teacher_script.heading: Recap and share one prior fact
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "We are continuing from Origins and Opening Acts. In one sentence please read your entry ticket aloud when I point to you. After three people, I will ask for one factual correction or addition." Point to student A, B, C to read. After three, say: "Quick class check: who can state one clear fact about the Storming of the Bastille or the role of the Estates General?" Accept one-sentence answers. If a student says 'the Estates General voted as one body', correct: "Remember: it met in three estates and how they voted was the dispute — we will return to that."

anticipated_questions: Why did the Third Estate declare itself the National Assembly?
Did the National Assembly cause the Bastille to be stormed?
Are the arrest and execution numbers exact?
teacher_script.board_action: Write dated sequence as bullets and the Reign of Terror definition and numbers.
teacher_script.heading: Teacher presentation: Estates General → National Assembly and dates
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Listen as I tell a short sequence of dated steps. I will point at the dates on the board. Follow along and underline any word you don't know." Read clearly: "May 1789: King summons the Estates General, a body that last met in 1614 and which had three estates — clergy, nobility, Third Estate. Voting procedures were contested: the Third Estate wanted to vote by head, not by estate. In June 1789 the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly, saying it represented the nation and would act as a constituent authority. Urban unrest followed, including the Storming of the Bastille in July, and the Assembly then moved to radical changes including the August Decrees." Then say: "Now a short factual overview of the Reign of Terror: from September 1793 to July 1794 revolutionary authorities arrested about 300,000 people and executed roughly 16,600 for counter-revolutionary activity. These are the numbers historians use as evidence; there are also different interpretations about why the Terror happened." Pause and ask: "Which date marks the start of the Terror? Which body declared itself in June 1789?"

anticipated_questions: How do we decide long-term vs short-term?
Can one cause be both long-term and short-term?
What counts as a good quote for evidence?
teacher_script.board_action: Write group labels: A: population growth, B: bad harvests, C: tax system, D: Enlightenment. Under each, leave space for students to add one quoted evidence line.
teacher_script.heading: Small-group source analysis: causes (long-term vs short-term)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Form groups of four. Each group gets one short extract to read: population growth; bad harvests and economic recession; tax system and resistance to reform; Enlightenment ideas. Read the extract aloud once (2 minutes). Then mark whether the extract describes a long-term cause or a short-term trigger and copy one line of evidence from the extract that supports your choice (6 minutes). I will circulate and listen to one group's reasoning. Be ready to report: your cause, long-term or short-term, and one quoted line as evidence (4 minutes)." Walk to groups, listen, and prompt with: "Which phrase shows time length? Where in the text does it say immediate impact?"

anticipated_questions: Can we use different evidence than our small-group extract?
Who were the moderates and who were the radicals?
Does debating mean we choose a side as our real belief?
teacher_script.board_action: Write debate roles and timing: "Moderates: statement 2', evidence 2', rebuttal 1' — Radicals: same."
teacher_script.heading: Structured role-play debate: moderates vs radicals
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Now split the class into two halves: moderates and radicals. Moderates argue that the National Assembly's steps were careful and did not justify extraordinary emergency measures. Radicals argue that the political crisis and threats made emergency measures likely. Use your group's evidence from the extracts: each side gets two minutes to state their main point and one piece of quoted evidence. Then each side gets one minute to rebut. Follow this script: statement (2 min), evidence read (2 min), rebuttal (1 min). I will time and call for the rebuttal. Begin." Circulate, remind students to name the cause they cite and to quote the line they used in the small-group activity. If students fall into the misconception that the Terror had united support, ask: "Where in our evidence do we see disagreements among revolutionaries?"

anticipated_questions: How long do the answers need to be?
Do I have to write dates for both answers?
What if I can't remember an exact phrase for evidence?
teacher_script.board_action: Write exit task instructions exactly as students must copy them.
teacher_script.heading: Check for understanding: exit questions
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "On a slip of paper, write three short answers: (1) List two causes of the Revolution and one short piece of evidence for each (one phrase each). (2) Write one dated step showing how the Estates General became the National Assembly (one line)." Collect slips or have students drop them in the tray. If a student writes only 'the Terror was supported by all revolutionaries,' ask them to add a line noting a division (for example, factions or Robespierre vs Hébertists)."

anticipated_questions: How long should the paragraph be?
Can we use class notes or must we quote the extract?
What if we disagree with the interpretations?
teacher_script.board_action: Write homework: "One-paragraph: pick one cause, cite one quote from today's extracts, explain link to later events. Due next class."
teacher_script.heading: Consolidate and assign homework
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "We covered the sequence from the Estates General to the National Assembly and the Reign of Terror's scope. Two interpretations stand out: (1) the Terror resulted from coherent central policy, and (2) it resulted from internal divisions, emergency pressures and contested decisions. For homework, write one paragraph citing one cause from today and explain, with one quoted line of evidence from today's extracts, how that cause helped lead to later events. That will prepare you for the Declaration of the Rights of Man next lesson." Repeat the homework exactly and tell students where to hand it in.

bullet_points: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen — issued by the National Assembly.
August Decrees: Legislation published by the Assembly that abolished feudalism and cancelled church tithes, and enacted equality before the law and other measures.

Civil Constitution of the Clergy (12 July 1790): Assembly confiscated church property, abolished tithes, and made clergy employees of the state; produced division and resistance among clergy and Catholics.
Example sequence: Estates-General → National Assembly → urban unrest (Bastille) → August Decrees.
Group questions: 1) What effects do the sources claim? 2) What voices or consequences are missing?
Class summary: Documents claim legal equality and state revenue; missing/competing views include loss of local religious authority, refusal of oath by many priests, and uneven benefits for peasants.
diagrams_to_draw: Simple arrow flow: Estates-General → National Assembly → Urban unrest (Bastille) → August Decrees (abolish feudalism, cancel tithes) → Confiscation of church property → Civil Constitution (clergy as state employees) → Social consequences (listed).
Two-column quick chart for debate: left column 'Priests / Peasants' (note: resistance, loss of income), right column 'Officials / Landowners' (note: revenue, sale of land).

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: They confiscated church property, cancelled/abolished tithes, and passed the Civil Constitution of the Clergy (which made clergy employees of the state). Any two of these are correct.
checkpoint_questions.question: Name two concrete measures the Assembly took against the Catholic Church described in this period.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: The class sources say these measures caused division and resistance among clergy and Catholics, unrest in parishes, and loss of trust in the Revolution — for example, priests refusing to accept state pay and peasants resisting reforms.
checkpoint_questions.question: According to the sources used in class, what is one social consequence the Assembly or its critics claimed followed from confiscating church property and abolishing tithes?

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: The excerpt downplays local peasant views and the practical impact of lost church charity; it may present the reform as orderly while ignoring violent resistance, émigré clergy, or how poorer people relied on the Church’s services.
checkpoint_questions.question: Give one silence or bias you can detect in the Civil Constitution excerpt we read (what the source does not show or downplays).

entry_ticket.expected_response: Common answer (misconception): "Peasants gain because they no longer pay tithes." A more accurate response: "The state and buyers of former church land gain money and power; many peasants may still lose local rights or face new rents or sell-offs; clergy lose status and income."
entry_ticket.prompt: If the National Assembly (1) cancels church tithes and (2) seizes church land to sell, who do you think immediately gains and who loses? Circle one: peasants / clergy / nobles / state. Then write one short reason for your choice (one sentence).

exit_ticket.prompt: Write one clear social consequence the class sources attribute to the Assembly’s church reforms (confiscation of property, abolition of tithes, Civil Constitution of the Clergy). Then give one alternative interpretation or a perspective the sources leave out.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Response names a social consequence linked to the reforms (for example: increased division/resistance among clergy and Catholics, parish unrest, loss of church charity) and then adds a plausible alternative or missing perspective (for example: peasants may have welcomed land redistribution; sources ignore women’s experience; the state’s administrative view).

homework.submission_format: Typed or handwritten paragraph plus citation; bring the quotation printed or written down.
tasks: Write a one-page (250–300 words) paragraph that: a) lists the three measures against the Church from class, b) explains one social consequence the sources attribute to those measures, and c) notes one perspective missing from those sources and why it matters.

Bring to class one short primary-source quotation (1–2 sentences) about the Church from a textbook or an online archive (cite the source). Be ready to say whether it supports or challenges the class sources.

mentor_moment.story: A history teacher once asked students whose grandparents had kept old family prayers. Several said those practices continued even when laws changed; people kept the ritual if it met daily needs.
mentor_moment.takeaway: Legal change can be swift, but social habits and local needs often determine how people actually respond.
mentor_moment.title: When reforms meet everyday needs

anticipated_questions: Student: "Which estate were parish priests in?" Anticipated: "Some parish priests were from the Third Estate; higher clergy were Second Estate."
Student: "Was the Bastille part of the Estates-General?" Anticipated: "No — the Bastille was an event of urban unrest that influenced the Assembly."
Student: "Do tithes apply to everyone?" Anticipated: "Tithes were payments to the Church that affected many peasants, but how they were enforced varied by region."
teacher_script.board_action: Write three one-line prompts for students to copy. Underline today: 'What the Assembly did to the Church; social consequences.'
teacher_script.heading: Activate prior knowledge and quick recap
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Take out your entry ticket answers. I will call three people to read one short line each: say who you circled and one reason. (Choose 3 volunteers.)" After each volunteer: "Quick check — which estate did clergy belong to? (Point at students: 'First, Second, or Third estate?')" Then ask three quick prompts aloud, waiting for thumbs-up/ thumbs-down: 1) "The Estates-General met because of a financial crisis — true or false?" 2) "The Third Estate claimed political representation — true or false?" 3) "Urban unrest (for example the storming of the Bastille) pushed the Assembly to act — true or false?" If a student answers false, ask them to say why briefly. Close: "Today we'll look at what the Assembly actually did to the Church and how people reacted."

anticipated_questions: Student: "Did the Assembly take property right away?" Anticipated: "The text says the Assembly confiscated church property — that was a legal action that then led to sales and redistribution."
Student: "What does 'employees of the state' mean for priests?" Anticipated: "It means priests would be paid by the state and required to swear loyalty to the Constitution, which many resisted."
Student: "Are the August Decrees the same as the Declaration?" Anticipated: "No — the Declaration is a statement of rights; the August Decrees are specific laws abolishing feudalism and tithes."
teacher_script.board_action: Write the three short headings and one quoted phrase under each: Declaration; August Decrees (use the exact definition); Civil Constitution of the Clergy (write 12 July 1790 and 'clergy employees of the state').
teacher_script.heading: Teacher-led evidence session: read key primary excerpts
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "I will read three short excerpts. Listen for actions taken and any stated reasons. After each reading I will ask one question." Read aloud (slowly, clearly): 1) A line introducing the Declaration: "The National Assembly issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen." Pause and ask: "What right or idea in the phrase 'Rights of Man and of the Citizen' might challenge church privilege?" 2) A line identifying the August Decrees: "August Decrees: Legislation published by the Assembly that abolished feudalism and cancelled church tithes, and enacted equality before the law and other measures." Pause and ask: "Which two concrete measures do you hear in that sentence?" 3) A short line on the Civil Constitution of the Clergy: "The Assembly confiscated church property, abolished tithes, and enacted the Civil Constitution of the Clergy (12 July 1790) making clergy employees of the state; this produced division and resistance among clergy and Catholics." Pause and ask: "What is one immediate legal change described here?" After the three, summarize aloud: "So the documents name (a) Declaration, (b) August Decrees ending feudal rights and tithes, and (c) seizure of church property plus Civil Constitution making clergy state employees."

anticipated_questions: Student: "What counts as a 'claimed effect'?" Anticipated: "Anything the source says will happen or be solved, for example 'equality before the law' or 'state revenue increases.'"
Student: "How do we identify bias?" Anticipated: "Look for who benefits in the text, who is named or unnamed, and whether the text admits problems or not."
Student: "Can we say a missing perspective is peasants even if not mentioned?" Anticipated: "Yes — if the source focuses on legal change but not daily life, peasants could be a missing perspective."
teacher_script.board_action: Write two guiding questions: '1) What effects do the sources claim follow from these measures?' '2) What voices or consequences are missing or understated?'
teacher_script.heading: Group source analysis (small groups)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Form groups of 3-4. Give each group two short excerpts: one describing confiscation/abolition of tithes and one from the Civil Constitution of the Clergy. Your task: (1) list two claimed effects these sources say will happen, and (2) name one thing the sources do not mention or might be biased about. Use the evidence in the excerpts to support your answers. I'll write two guiding questions on the board. You have 10 minutes to discuss and 2 minutes to write a quick public note to post on the wall." Walk among groups, prompt with: "Where does the document say the money goes? Who might oppose this change and why?" If a group gets stuck, read a sentence from the excerpt and ask them to underline the verbs.

anticipated_questions: Student (priest role): "Can we say all peasants resisted?" Anticipated: "You should say some peasants resisted while others accepted changes; use evidence or note silence."
Student (official role): "Did selling land help the national budget right away?" Anticipated: "The sources claim revenue, but students may question timing and distribution."
Student in audience: "Are priests allowed to refuse being state employees?" Anticipated: "Many priests refused to swear the oath; that refusal created division and resistance among Catholics."
teacher_script.board_action: Draw two columns titled 'Priests/Peasants' and 'Officials/Landowners' and quickly jot one evidence phrase each side cites during presentations.
teacher_script.heading: Role-play debate: social consequences and resistance
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Two larger groups will present: Group A = parish priests and Catholic peasants; Group B = revolutionary officials and landowners. Each side has 3 minutes total: 1 minute to state your main claim, 2 minutes to cite one piece of evidence from the excerpts and answer a quick question from me. Start with Group A." Call on the two spokespersons. After each short presentation ask one pointed question: to priests/peasants: "Which social consequence worried you most?" to officials/landowners: "How did you justify selling church land to gain revenue?" Remind both sides to use the excerpt evidence and to note where sources skip a viewpoint.

anticipated_questions: Student: "Can my alternative be about the economy?" Anticipated: "Yes — an economic or social missing perspective is valid if you explain why it's missing from the sources."

Student: "Will these disagreements cause the Terror?" Anticipated: "They help explain some causes of later repression, but the next lesson will show the direct links and specific laws like the Law of 22 Prairial."
Student: "Do we hand in the exit sentence?" Anticipated: "Yes, I will collect these as the individual exit ticket."
teacher_script.board_action: Under the two columns add a final line: 'Class sources: legal equality, revenue, end of tithes' and 'Missing/competing views: local unrest, religious division, uneven benefit.'
teacher_script.heading: Individual check + teacher consolidation and bridge
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Write one clear social consequence the class sources attribute to the church reforms (one sentence). Then write one alternative interpretation or a perspective the sources miss (one sentence)." Give 3 minutes writing time. After 3 minutes collect a few samples aloud: read 2 student answers (one that follows the sources and one that offers a missing perspective). Finish with a 1-minute summary: "Competing interpretations: Documents present legal changes and claim equality and revenue. Critics and many clergy saw loss of religious freedom and local stability. Those disagreements help explain later repression during the Terror and the Thermidor reaction."

bullet_points: Examples students named: higher expectations; church reforms anger; land disputes; political enemies
Drownings at Nantes — primary account: mass executions by drowning (method highlighted)
Law of 22 Prairial (1794): denied accused 'enemies of the people' the right to defend themselves
Robespierre: arrested, taken to Hotel de Ville, injured after attempting suicide, executed 28 July
Group A claim — (example) 'executions were widespread' — Evidence: drownings; Reign of Terror stats — Alternative: local actions, not central plan
Group B claim — (example) '22 Prairial sped up executions' — Evidence: law text 'no defence'; increased tribunal speed — Alternative: law responded to emergency fears
Group C claim — (example) 'Robespierre lost support' — Evidence: arrest narrative; factions vs him — Alternative: personal rivals used repression to remove him
Certainties: Terror involved mass executions; 22 Prairial removed legal defence rights; Robespierre was arrested and executed 28 July
Contested: the exact scale (numerical estimates); whether repression had unified leadership; precise motives for Thermidor
Leads to Thermidor/Directory: reaction against repression; divisions among revolutionaries opened path to new regime
diagrams_to_draw: Simple timeline: '22 Prairial (June 1794) → Arrest/execution (28 July 1794)' with arrows linking 'Law' to 'accelerated tribunal decisions' to 'executions'.

Column comparison: left column 'Evidence' (drownings, law text, arrest account) vs right column 'Interpretations' (central policy vs local violence; legal change = acceleration vs emergency measure; fall = loss of support vs political purge).
headings: Links from earlier reforms → rising tensions
Group headings: A Scale of deaths | B Law of 22 Prairial | C Why Robespierre fell

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Evidence 1: Accounts of drownings at Nantes — these describe mass, local executions carried out by representatives and local officials, showing repression could be organised outside Paris. Evidence 2: Text or summary of the Law of 22 Prairial — this law removed defendants' rights to defend themselves in Paris trials, showing a central legal change that sped up executions. Each shows a different mechanism: local massacres and centralised legal acceleration.
checkpoint_questions.question: Using the primary-source extracts on drownings at Nantes and the Law of 22 Prairial, which pieces of evidence would you use to support a claim that the Terror involved both local violence and central legal changes? Give two pieces of evidence and explain briefly how each supports the claim.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Best fit: the documents show political divisions and inconsistent policy. Supporting detail: evidence of conflict between revolutionary factions (e.g., references to Hébertists vs moderates, or differing accounts of Robespierre's motives and actions) and the narrative of Robespierre losing support before Thermidor suggests internal disagreement rather than total unity. Alternatively, if a student chooses the unified-policy view, they must cite high execution statistics plus the Law of 22 Prairial as centralising force.
checkpoint_questions.question: One historian argues the high death toll estimates show a unified revolutionary policy of mass extermination; another argues the evidence shows political divisions and inconsistent policy. Which interpretation fits the documents you studied best, and what is one specific document detail that supports that interpretation?

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Explanation: Robespierre's arrest and execution show he had lost support among other revolutionaries, so Thermidor can be seen as a political reaction against his leadership and policies. Limitation: the episode alone doesn't prove broader public opinion or structural factors (war, economic strain, provincial resistance) caused Thermidor; it may reflect elite power struggles more than wider causes.
checkpoint_questions.question: Explain briefly how Robespierre's arrest and execution (as described in the extracts) can be used to explain a cause of Thermidor. State one limitation of using that episode alone to explain the end of the Terror.

entry_ticket.expected_response: A useful response names one of: a single leader (e.g. Robespierre), a committee or groups (e.g. Committee of Public Safety, local Revolutionary Tribunals), or many officials (local representatives, municipal authorities). The underlined certainty should reveal students' confidence (common wrong answer: 'definitely a single leader' which signals the misconception of unified control).
entry_ticket.prompt: Write one short sentence answering: "Who decided to execute people during the Terror — a single leader, a group, or many different officials?" Then underline the one word that shows how sure you are (e.g., definitely, probably, maybe).

exit_ticket.prompt: Write a short analytical paragraph (4–6 sentences) that answers: To what extent did the Law of 22 Prairial change how the Terror worked, and how does this compare with evidence of local violent practices like the drownings at Nantes? Use at least one specific detail from the documents.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Paragraph states a clear judgement about the Law of 22 Prairial's impact (e.g., it accelerated judicial executions by removing defence rights) and compares that central legal change to local practices (e.g., drownings at Nantes were extra-legal or locally organised). Includes at least one specific document detail (date/name of law; a phrase or fact about Nantes drownings) and a sentence noting a limitation or alternative interpretation (e.g., internal divisions or differing scales).

homework.submission_format: Written paragraphs (digital or handwritten scanned PDF).
tasks: Write a one-page (≈250–350 words) answer to: 'Which mattered more in increasing executions during the Terror — legal changes like the Law of 22 Prairial or local acts of violence? Use two pieces of evidence from the period's documents and explain an alternate interpretation.'

Select one primary-source extract from today's set and annotate it: underline two phrases that show perspective or bias, write one sentence on the author's possible motive, and one sentence on how that affects using the extract as evidence.

mentor_moment.story: A historian once showed a classroom two lists: one of laws passed in Paris and one of local letters reporting massacres. Students realised the laws looked neat but the letters showed messy fights and fear on the ground.
mentor_moment.takeaway: Laws tell you what leaders intended; local accounts show what actually happened. Use both to reach a balanced judgement.
mentor_moment.title: When paperwork hid the fights

anticipated_questions: Can I change my ticket answer after talking? (Yes — we revise ideas in history.)
Do you mean all reforms caused repression? (No — tell me which reform and why you think it raised tensions.)
Should I use dates? (Not yet — focus on links between reform and tension.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write 4 short phrases from student shares, e.g. 'higher expectations', 'church changes → anger', 'land disputes', 'political enemies'.
teacher_script.heading: Activate prior knowledge: link earlier reforms to rising tensions
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Take out your entry ticket. I will give you 90 seconds to compare answers with a neighbour and choose the clearest one sentence to share. Then each pair will tell us one link between earlier revolutionary reform and the pressure that could lead to repression. Speak quickly: one pair, one link." After pairs share, ask: "What patterns do you hear? Who said that reforms raised expectations? Who said they created enemies for the revolution?" Call on 4 pairs to say their link and write one or two words from each on the board.

anticipated_questions: Is the drowning account true? (The extract claims it; historians debate scale and context — that's why we compare sources.)
Was the Law of 22 Prairial a single day law? (Yes—dated 22 Prairial 1794; we use the exact wording from the document.)
Did Robespierre die the same day he was arrested? (The extract says he was arrested, taken to Hotel de Ville, injured after attempting suicide, and executed on 28 July.)
teacher_script.board_action: Add short labels under the earlier phrases: next to 'land disputes' write 'evidence: drownings at Nantes'; add a new line: 'Law of 22 Prairial — no defence'; add 'Robespierre: arrested, injured, executed 28 July'.
teacher_script.heading: Introduce new material: evidence tour of the Terror
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "We're going to look at short extracts. I'll read each extract aloud, show where it came from, and model how to weigh claims." Read Extract 1: a short account describing drownings at Nantes (read two sentences that describe mass executions by drownings). Then point: "What claim does this extract make about the scale or method of repression?" Ask one student to summarise in one sentence. Next read Extract 2: the Law of 22 Prairial excerpt (read the sentence that says it denied accused the right to defend themselves). Ask: "What does this change do to legal protection?" Write the phrase 'no defence' on the board. Finally read Extract 3: an account of Robespierre's arrest and execution (read the lines about Hotel de Ville, attempted suicide injury, execution on 28 July). Model weighing: say aloud, "This source gives a precise sequence of events — arrest, injury, execution — but it doesn't tell us why he lost support. We must compare it to other accounts." Ask students to whisper one word describing whether each extract is eyewitness, law text, or later history. Collect answers.

anticipated_questions: Do we need to use other sources? (Use only the extracts we just read and what we've learned previously.)
What's an alternative interpretation? (A reasonable different explanation based on the same documents — e.g., deaths were local actions not central policy.)
How formal should the argument be? (Short and clear: one sentence claim, two brief evidence points, one alternative.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write headings for groups: A Scale of deaths; B Law of 22 Prairial; C Why Robespierre fell. Under each, write 'Claim — Evidence — Alternative'.
teacher_script.heading: Practise interpretation: jigsaw group work
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Form three jigsaw groups. Group A: scale of deaths (use the drownings extract and Reign of Terror statistics). Group B: Law of 22 Prairial's legal effects (use the law excerpt). Group C: motives for Robespierre's fall (use the arrest/execution account and the note about lost support). Each group has 8 minutes to prepare a 90-second argument: one main claim, two pieces of evidence from the extracts, and one alternative interpretation you might expect. I'll time you. Use this worksheet: Claim / Evidence 1 / Evidence 2 / Alternative view." Circulate and prompt: "Show me the two words you'll say for your evidence. Who in your group will state the alternative interpretation?" Give a 2-minute warning and bring class back.

anticipated_questions: Can the critic use outside facts? (Keep to the documents and what we've studied earlier.)
What if we run out of time to answer? (Keep answers short — one sentence.)
Is disagreement allowed? (Yes — historians expect competing interpretations.)
teacher_script.board_action: During each presentation, write the group's one-sentence claim and the two evidence words under its heading. Note one challenge raised by the critic next to it.
teacher_script.heading: Check whether it landed: structured debate and role-play
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Each group presents its 90-second argument. After each, one student from another group will play a contemporary critic and ask one question; the presenting group answers. I'll ask one follow-up that focuses on causation or perspective." Run presentations in order A, B, C. After each presentation, prompt the critic: 'Why might someone disagree?' Then ask the class: 'Does this evidence prove a single cause or multiple causes?' Press for specifics: 'Which sentence in your evidence supports that claim?'

anticipated_questions: Can we copy the board for notes? (Yes — copy the certainties and contested points.)
Do we have to decide now if the Terror was justified? (No — we are analysing causes and evidence, not making moral judgements here.)
Will this be on the test? (You'll be assessed on interpreting evidence and comparing interpretations.)
teacher_script.board_action: Under the three group headings, add two columns labeled 'Certainties' and 'Contested'. Add final line: 'Leads to Thermidor/Directory: loss of revolutionary unity; reaction against repression.'
teacher_script.heading: Consolidate: whole-class synthesis
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Let's list what we can all agree on (certainties), what remains contested, and the link to Thermidor and the Directory. I'll call for one certainty, one contested point, and one way this leads to Thermidor from different students." Guide them: write 'Certainties' then 'Contested' then 'Leads to...'. Aim for 2 items each. Close: "Remember our objective: we practiced analysing the scale and mechanisms of repression and weighing different interpretations — historians rarely get a single answer; they weigh evidence and argument." End with: "Tonight: jot one sentence in your notes answering whether the Terror was unified or divided; we'll use it next lesson."

bullet_points: Thermidor: Robespierre executed; reprisals in southern France
Law of 22 Prairial: faster trials, limited defence rights
Bicameral legislature: Council of 500 and Council of Ancients
Executive: Five Directors (the Directory)
Elections: indirect; property qualifications for voting/office
Stabilising (quote): restored order, checked Jacobins
Oligarchic rollback (quote): property rules excluded many; favoured elites
Group task: 2 pieces of evidence for each view from the two excerpts
Role prompts: Director — order & defence; Jacobin — oligarchy & exclusion; Rural delegate — local impact & conscription
Exit ticket: evidence for each view + question for next lesson
diagrams_to_draw: Simple chart: top box 'Directory (1795)' with arrows down to two boxes: 'Council of 500' and 'Council of Ancients' and a side box 'Five Directors (executive)'
Timeline strip: 1792 Insurrection (10 Aug) → Republic proclaimed Sept 1792 → Louis XVI executed Jan 1793 → 1795 Constitution (Year III) → Directory period

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Property qualifications and indirect elections limited who chose legislators and directors, which reduced rapid swings in popular opinion and made governments more predictable; that stability helped prevent immediate returns to terror or royalist chaos by keeping power with moderate propertied groups.
checkpoint_questions.question: Look at the Constitution of Year III's institutions (bicameral legislature and five-director executive). How could property qualifications for voting and indirect elections make the Directory more stabilising to the Republic? Give one clear causal reason.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Evidence repression continued: revenge killings in southern France after Thermidor show ongoing local violence. Evidence of moving away from Terror: many Jacobin leaders were removed from power and Robespierre was executed, showing the central government repudiated the Terror's leadership.
checkpoint_questions.question: Name one piece of evidence from the period after Thermidor that suggests repression continued, and one piece that suggests the Revolution was moving away from Terror. State each briefly.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Mass mobilisation created a large military bureaucracy and dependence on army success, so the Directory could use military recruitment, victories, and patronage to secure support and suppress internal unrest, tying military interests to the regime's survival.
checkpoint_questions.question: The Revolutionary Wars mobilised mass armies and created satellite states. Explain in one sentence how war mobilisation could strengthen the Directory's control inside France.

entry_ticket.expected_response: A should be chosen. Correct answer: A — southern France had revenge killings and reprisals, while some former Terror figures kept positions, so removal was not immediate or complete. If a student chooses B, that shows the misconception that the Terror ended with a complete purge of its personnel.
entry_ticket.prompt:
Circle the statement you think is truer after Thermidor (choose one) and write one short reason (1 sentence):
A) Southern France saw revenge killings and reprisals against suspected Terror supporters.
B) All former Terror officials were immediately removed from office across France.
Which did you pick and why?

exit_ticket.prompt: Write one specific piece of evidence from today's documents or lecture that supports the interpretation that the Directory stabilised the Republic, and one specific piece of evidence that supports the interpretation that the Directory represented an oligarchic rollback. Finally, write one focused question you want answered next lesson about the abolition of slavery or revolutionary propaganda.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Student lists (a) one concrete evidence for 'stabilising' (e.g., property qualifications, bicameral legislature, removal of Terror leaders) and explains in one line how it implies stability; (b) one concrete evidence for 'oligarchic rollback' (e.g., voting restrictions, directors drawn from propertied classes, limits on popular participation) and explains in one line how it implies rollback; and (c) one clear, lesson-related question about abolition or propaganda that could be answered by primary sources or next lesson content.

homework.submission_format: Two short annotated excerpts (uploaded or photocopied) and the 3-minute summary as 3–5 bullet points.
tasks: Read a short primary excerpt (provided) of the Directory's voting qualification law. Highlight one phrase that supports the 'oligarchic rollback' interpretation and write one sentence explaining why.
Read a one-paragraph eyewitness account (provided) of conscription orders. In two sentences, explain how that account supports the idea that war mobilisation expanded state power.

Prepare one 3-minute summary (bullet points acceptable) answering: Based on today's evidence, which interpretation of the Directory do you find more convincing and why? Use two pieces of evidence from class documents.

mentor_moment.story: A teacher once told students how a single rule about who could vote in post-revolutionary France shifted debates in every town: landlords met more often at council meetings, and poorer delegates stopped being invited. That tiny legal change changed who made decisions.
mentor_moment.takeaway: Small rules—like who may vote—can change who holds power and what counts as 'stability.'
mentor_moment.title: When a small rule changes everything

anticipated_questions: Did Robespierre die immediately in Thermidor or later? (Answer: executed in Thermidor month.)
Why were there reprisals only in the south? (Answer: regional tensions and local conflicts; not uniform across France.)
If Law of 22 Prairial made trials faster, did that mean fewer lawyers? (Answer: it limited defence rights and simplified proceedings.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write two short bullets: "Thermidor: Robespierre executed; reprisals in south" and "Law of 22 Prairial: faster trials, harsher repression"
teacher_script.heading: Recap Thermidor and Law of 22 Prairial
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Quick recap — two facts. First: Thermidor means Robespierre fell and was executed. Ask the class: name one consequence we discussed last lesson. Wait for answers and name-check: insurrections, arrests, reprisals in the south. Second: remind students of the Law of 22 Prairial — who remembers the main effect? (Prompt: faster trials, fewer defenses.)" Then read aloud two concrete examples from last lesson: "Reprisals in the south included killings of suspected Terror supporters; but some former Terror officials kept posts in local government."

anticipated_questions: What does 'indirect elections' mean here? (Answer: voters chose electors who then chose officials.)
How high were the property qualifications? (Answer: the text doesn't give a number in this lesson; recognise inequality in access.)
Were the Directors like modern presidents? (Answer: not exactly — they were a collective five-person executive.)
teacher_script.board_action: Add heading: "Constitution of Year III (1795)" and list: "- Bicameral: Council of 500; Council of Ancients  - Five Directors (executive)  - Indirect elections; property qualifications" Add two quoted one-line historian views labeled: "Stabilising" and "Oligarchic rollback"
teacher_script.heading: Teacher-led evidence: Constitution of Year III and Directory
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Now we look at how the Revolution changed its institutions in 1795. I'll summarise key points from the Constitution of Year III. Listen for: structure, how leaders were chosen, and who could vote." Read each point clearly: "It created a bicameral legislature: the Council of 500 and the Council of Ancients. It set a five-person executive, the Directory. Elections were indirect and there were property qualifications for office and voting." Then display two short historian quotations (read them): Quote 1 (stabilising view): "Some historians argue the Directory restored order by checking Jacobin power and limiting terror." Quote 2 (critical view): "Others say property qualifications produced an oligarchic rollback that shut out poor citizens." Ask: "Which quotation fits our prior examples of reprisals and retained officials?" Wait for quick responses.

anticipated_questions: Can we use the textbook? (Answer: Use only the provided excerpts for evidence.)
What counts as a piece of evidence? (Answer: a direct phrase, rule, or order from the excerpt that supports an interpretation.)
Do we need to agree on one interpretation? (Answer: No — list evidence for both; the class will debate perspectives.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write instructions: "Group task: 2 pieces of evidence for each view (stabilising vs oligarchic). 9 min work + 2 min report."
teacher_script.heading: Small-group document analysis
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Form groups of three. Each group gets two short excerpts: one about property qualifications for voting/office, and one a military mobilisation order. Your task: list two pieces of evidence that support each interpretation — (A) 'Directory stabilised the Republic' and (B) 'Directory was an oligarchic rollback.' Use the documents only. You have 9 minutes to read and make a 2-bullet list for each interpretation, then pick one person to give a 2-minute position." Hand out the excerpts. Walk the room, ask groups: 'Which phrase in the property rule sounds exclusionary?' or 'What in the mobilisation order suggests mass conscription or central control?' After 9 minutes call time and ask groups to prepare their 2-minute position.

anticipated_questions: Can we read directly from our notes during the role-play? (Answer: Yes, quote your evidence.)
What if our group disagrees about what the document says? (Answer: pick one line you can all cite; role-play can show conflict.)
Will everyone play a role? (Answer: We'll rotate; first three groups go now so others watch and prepare.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write role prompts briefly: "Director: order & defence; Jacobin: oligarchy & exclusion; Rural: local harm & conscription impact"
teacher_script.heading: Role-play Council simulation
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Now we do a 6-minute simulation. Three roles at a time: a Director, a Jacobin critic, and a rural delegate. The topic: should conscription be enforced and should property-based voting remain? Directors defend order; Jacobins argue danger of oligarchy; rural delegate speaks for local impact. Each role has 1 minute to speak. Use evidence from your group work. I'll ring a bell after each minute and then we take one quick clap and move to the next trio. I'll call three groups to go first." Give quick role prompts on a sheet: Director — emphasise stability, national defence; Jacobin — emphasise political exclusion, threats to popular sovereignty; Rural delegate — emphasise local reprisals, effects of conscription. Circulate and prompt: "Which line from your excerpt would your role quote?"

anticipated_questions: Do the evidence lines have to be quotes? (Answer: A short paraphrase from the documents is fine; show which excerpt it came from.)
Can I ask a procedural question next lesson? (Answer: Yes — ask about any of the listed upcoming topics.)
How will you use our questions? (Answer: We'll group them and start next lesson with the most common ones.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write exit ticket instructions exactly: "1) Evidence for 'stabilising'  2) Evidence for 'oligarchic rollback'  3) One question for next lesson (abolition, propaganda, or women's roles)"
teacher_script.heading: Exit ticket: consolidate evidence and question
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Write an exit ticket: one piece of evidence that supports 'Directory stabilised the Republic' and one piece of evidence that supports 'Directory was an oligarchic rollback.' Then write one question you want answered next lesson about abolition, propaganda, or women's roles. (Two evidence lines + one question.) You have 4 minutes. Turn in on the way out."

bullet_points: Prompts: Newspapers & pamphlets | Guillotine | La Marseillaise | Assignats | Abolition & women
1) Abolition — 'Amid revolts ... the Convention abolished slavery in the colonies on 4 February 1794 and granted full rights regardless of colour.'
2) Assignats — 'Paper currency backed by nationalised church and émigré lands.' Note: over-issuance → hyperinflation and economic disruption.
3) Pamphlets/newspapers — 'proliferated during the Revolution, becoming the main communication medium and stimulating revolutionary debate.'

4) Symbols & women — 'La Marseillaise: A song composed in 1792 ... adopted ... in 1795.' 'Guillotine: an execution device ... principal symbol of the Terror.' 'Women: initially participated in activism ... 1791 and 1793 constitutions denied them political rights; women's clubs were banned in October 1793.'
Group table columns: Group | Quote used | Alternative interpretation (students fill during activity)
Debate motions: 1) Newspapers/pamphlets were the main cause of rapid change after Thermidor. 2) Assignats mattered more for daily life than symbols.
Follow-up readings: Britannica (overview), Chisick (pamphlets), Opie (guillotine), Acemoglu et al. (consequences of reform)
diagrams_to_draw: Simple timeline: mark 1791 (constitution denies women political rights), Oct 1793 (women's clubs banned), 4 Feb 1794 (abolition decree), 1795 (La Marseillaise adopted).
Flow diagram for assignats: nationalised church & émigré lands → backing for assignats (paper currency) → over-issuance → hyperinflation → economic disruption.
Two-column sketch: 'Symbol' (guillotine, anthem) vs 'Policy/Material' (assignats, abolition decree) with arrow to 'Public experience' to show competing interpretations.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Newspapers and pamphlets spread arguments quickly and shaped public opinion. The student should cite a passage from the lesson that shows a pamphlet/newspaper framing a debate (for example, a quoted newspaper passage that criticised Directory policy or urged action on abolition). The answer must name the mechanism (rapid circulation and public persuasion) and give the quoted/example passage from the period text as evidence.
checkpoint_questions.question: Using the document passages you read, name one way newspapers or pamphlets changed political debate during the Revolution and cite the specific example given in the period text.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Assignats were paper currency backed by nationalised church and émigré lands. The problem was over-issuance: the government printed too many assignats, causing inflation and economic disruption, as described in the period text.
checkpoint_questions.question: Explain briefly how assignats were supposed to work and then state the problem identified in the document that made them disrupt the economy.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: (a) One interpretation: the guillotine became a symbol because it was a visible, public instrument tied to the Terror and to ideas of equal, legal execution. (b) One interpretation: women were excluded because the 1791 and 1793 constitutions denied them political rights and authorities later banned women's clubs; another interpretation notes fears about social order and men's control of politics. The student should state one interpretation for each and, if possible, refer to the document's phrasing about bans and constitutions.
checkpoint_questions.question: The document gives competing interpretations about the guillotine and women's political roles. Give one interpretation for each: (a) why the guillotine became a powerful symbol, and (b) why women were excluded from formal politics.

entry_ticket.expected_response: Most correct students pick B and may add: 'Because the Convention declared abolition and equal rights for colonies on 4 Feb 1794.' A common wrong answer is A; students who pick A often believe legal abolition meant instant, universal freedom in practice. That mistake helps us discuss limits between law and implementation.
entry_ticket.prompt:
Below are four short statements. Circle the one that you think is true after the Revolution's 1794 decree. Only one is correct.
A) Slavery was abolished everywhere in the French empire and all enslaved people were immediately free in practice.
B) The Convention abolished slavery in the colonies on 4 February 1794 and granted full rights regardless of colour.
C) The 1794 decree applied only to enslaved people who served in the army.
D) The 1794 decree made slave owners keep their property but pay wages to formerly enslaved people.
Write the letter you chose and one sentence saying why.

exit_ticket.prompt: Using a specific passage from the period text, explain in one short paragraph how newspapers or pamphlets influenced public debate during the Revolution and identify the exact example (the quoted line or passage) you used.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: A correct response names a causal claim about newspapers/pamphlets (they spread arguments, shaped opinion, pressured leaders, or framed issues), includes a quoted line or clearly cited passage from the lesson text as evidence, and links that quote to the claim in one or two sentences.

homework.submission_format: typed paragraph and citation (or handwritten if necessary)
tasks: Write a one-page (about 250 words) paragraph that uses two quotations from the period text to argue either that assignats harmed the economy or that newspapers strengthened revolutionary debate. Underline the two quotations and explain in one sentence why each supports your argument.

Find one secondary source listed in the upcoming readings (Britannica, Opie, Acemoglu et al., or Chisick). Bring the citation and one sentence saying which thread from today (abolition, newspapers, symbols, women, or assignats) that reading will likely deepen.

mentor_moment.story: A local teacher once told students how a short pamphlet, printed and handed out before a town meeting, swung the vote by putting one clear example at the top. People remembered the example more than abstract arguments.
mentor_moment.takeaway: When you pick one clear passage as evidence and explain how it would persuade someone, your history argument becomes stronger and easier to remember.
mentor_moment.title: When a Pamphlet Changed a Vote

anticipated_questions: Do you want facts or opinions in the pair share? (Either is fine; we want what you already believe.)
Should we write our ideas on the board? (No—just tell your partner; we'll collect a few aloud.)
If I don't remember anything about one topic, can I skip it? (Yes—say what you do know.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write five short prompts down the left side of the board: 1) Newspapers & pamphlets 2) Guillotine 3) La Marseillaise 4) Assignats 5) Abolition & women. Add next to each the word 'One thing you know'.
teacher_script.heading: Activate prior knowledge: quick recap and paired share
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: 'Turn to the person next to you. In one minute, list aloud three things you remember from our last period: Thermidor, the Directory, or war mobilisation. Then spend two minutes listing anything you know about these five topics: newspapers/pamphlets, the guillotine, La Marseillaise, assignats, abolition of slavery, and women's political role. I will call on two pairs to share one point each.' After 1 minute, say: 'Switch; now focus on the five topics.' Call on two pairs: ask each to name which of the five they discussed.

anticipated_questions: Did the abolition apply to Saint-Domingue only? (The passage says 'the colonies.' We will discuss limits between law and practice.)
Were assignats backed by land or by the state? (The passage: 'backed by nationalised church and émigré lands.')
Was the guillotine invented before the Terror? (The passage links it to the Revolution and to the Terror as a principal symbol.)
Did women lose rights in 1791 or 1793? (Both: constitutions denied political rights; clubs banned Oct 1793.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write four numbered quote boxes on the board, each with a short label and a one-line quote from the passage: 1) Abolition — 'abolished slavery... 4 February 1794' 2) Assignats — 'paper currency backed by nationalised church and émigré lands' (+ note: 'over-issuance → inflation') 3) Pamphlets — 'proliferated... stimulating revolutionary debate' 4) Symbols & women — 'La Marseillaise...1795'; 'guillotine...principal symbol of the Terror'; 'women's clubs banned Oct 1793.'
teacher_script.heading: Introduce new material: evidence walk-through
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: 'I'll read four short passages aloud. Listen for one concrete fact you can quote.' Read passage 1 slowly: 'Amid revolts and military actions in Saint-Domingue and other colonies, the Convention abolished slavery in the colonies on 4 February 1794 and granted full rights regardless of colour.' Pause and ask: 'What exact phrase would you quote to show legal abolition?' Point at volunteers. Read passage 2: 'Assignats: paper currency backed by nationalised church and émigré lands.' Ask: 'What problem followed the policy?' If no answer, add: 'Over-issuance caused hyperinflation and economic disruption.' Read passage 3: 'Newspapers and pamphlets proliferated during the Revolution, becoming the main communication medium and stimulating revolutionary debate.' Ask: 'Give one short quote we could use as evidence that pamphlets shaped debate.' Read passage 4: 'La Marseillaise: A song composed in 1792 that was adopted by the National Convention as the First Republic's anthem in 1795. Guillotine: An execution device invented during the Revolution, regarded as the principal symbol of the Terror. Women: initially participated in activism and organised societies, but the 1791 and 1793 constitutions denied them political rights and women's clubs were banned in October 1793.' After reading, ask: 'Which of these passages shows contested interpretations? Say yes or no: guillotine symbolism? women's role?'

anticipated_questions: Can two groups use the same passage? (Yes.)
Do we have to act out a historical person? (No — focus on argument and evidence.)
What counts as an alternative interpretation? (Any different explanation for the same evidence, e.g. law vs. implementation.)
teacher_script.board_action: Add a small table with three columns labeled: Group, Quote used, Alternative interpretation. Leave rows for groups to copy later.
teacher_script.heading: Practice: small-group role-play & evidence task
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: 'Form groups of three. Each group chooses one role: (A) pamphleteer/newspaper editor arguing a claim about abolition or assignats or women's clubs; or (B) Directory official defending a policy. Your job: in six minutes, write a 2-3 sentence argument and cite one passage we just read as evidence. Also write one alternative interpretation someone might give. I'll circulate. After six minutes prepare to read your argument aloud in 30 seconds.' Circulate: prompt groups with questions: 'Which exact words will you quote? Who might disagree and why? How did newspapers make your voice reach people?' If stuck, point to the quote boxes and say 'use this exact line.'

anticipated_questions: How strict is the 30–40 seconds? (Be brief — we need everyone to speak.)
Can we read our sentences exactly as written? (Yes.)
If our alternative interpretation is weak, can we change it on the spot? (Yes — briefly.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write short two-column live notes after each group: 'Quote used' and 'Alt interpretation' — update the table started earlier.
teacher_script.heading: Check for understanding: rapid group presentations
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: 'Each group has 30–40 seconds. Name your role, read your 2–3 sentence argument, and quote the exact passage you used. End by naming one alternative interpretation. I'll time you.' After each presentation, ask one targeted question to the presenting group: 'Does that passage show cause or just a decision? Who bears the consequences?' Use students' answers to probe causation (e.g., law vs. implementation) and perspective (whose voice is missing).

anticipated_questions: Do we have to read all the follow-up sources? (You will be assigned specific ones; I just showed which deepen each thread.)
Can the guillotine be both a symbol and a practical tool? (Yes — that's an example of competing interpretations you should notice.)
Will this debate affect the next assessment? (Yes — you'll use passages like the ones we quoted to support claims.)
teacher_script.board_action: Under the table, write two motion headings and leave space for one-line pro/con notes. At the bottom, write the three follow-up readings matched to the threads: Britannica (overview), Chisick (pamphlets), Opie (guillotine), Acemoglu et al. (consequences of reform).
teacher_script.heading: Consolidate: whole-class debate and synthesis
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: 'We'll close with a 5-minute debate linking symbols, media, and economic policy. I'll pose two motions; we'll vote after quick reasons. Motion 1: "Newspapers and pamphlets were the main cause of rapid political change after Thermidor." Motion 2: "Economic policy (assignats) mattered more for people's daily experience than symbols like the guillotine or anthem." For each motion, ask for one pro and one con from different students, requiring each to cite one passage or example from our board. After votes, summarise: point out where evidence is strong, where interpretations disagree (law vs. practice; symbol as cultural vs. political), and say: 'For next class, read the Britannica article and Chisick on pamphlets to see more evidence on the role of press; Opie on the guillotine for symbolism; Acemoglu et al. for economic consequences.' End: 'Write down one sentence that links media, symbols, or assignats to what you think mattered most to ordinary people.'

bullet_points: Student examples: (copy 3 from entry tickets)
Model marks: underline = claim; circle = concrete example; note audience
Group task: 1) List 2 pieces of evidence (quote or line #) 2) Write 1 alternative interpretation
Roles: publisher, royalist critic, popular reader, historian
Debate prompt: Did the pamphlet change outcomes or reflect opinion? Cite 1 evidence + 1 counter-interpretation
Synthesis: Evidence can show influence OR reflection — weigh both
Key citations to consult: Britannica (French Revolution), Opie (Guillotine), Chisick (pamphlets), Acemoglu et al. (2011)
diagrams_to_draw: A two-column chart labeled 'Evidence for influence' and 'Alternative interpretation' with two example rows
Underline and circle demo on the quoted passage (one short line underlined, one phrase circled)

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: One-sentence influence claim naming the pamphlet/newspaper and the concrete example from the passage (for example: "The pamphlet accused local officials of hoarding grain and called for public inspections, which would push readers to demand investigations"). One-sentence alternative interpretation that cites the same passage and explains how it might report existing popular anger or copy other sources (for example: "Alternatively, the pamphlet may simply be reflecting already widespread complaints about grain prices and amplifying them, not originating them").
checkpoint_questions.question: Pick the short passage your group annotated. Write one sentence that shows how the pamphlet (or newspaper) in that passage tried to change what people believed or did. Then write one sentence offering a different explanation for the same passage (it reflected opinion rather than caused it).

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: The student names the example used in the modelled passage (e.g., a named pamphlet, a quoted call for action, an instance of a riot or petition) and explains the link in one line (e.g., "The pamphlet's open call to join petitions links printed rhetoric to collective action because readers later formed those petitions").
checkpoint_questions.question: From the teacher-modelled passage (Chisick/Britannica), identify the concrete example the author uses to show media influence. Say in one line how that example functions as evidence (what it links).

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Pro-argument: a concise statement tying printed debate to policy or institutional change (for example: "Printed debates spread new ideas that altered political coalitions, helping reforms pass, which Acemoglu et al. link to institutional change"). Contra-argument: a concise statement questioning causation or pointing to structural forces (for example: "Alternatively, structural economic pressures and elite choices, not pamphlets, may have driven reforms, so printed media were secondary").
checkpoint_questions.question: Using Acemoglu et al. as discussed at the end of class, give one short reason a historian might argue that pamphlets mattered for long-term consequences of the Revolution, and one short reason a historian might doubt that claim.

entry_ticket.expected_response: Two short examples (e.g., "pamphlet: Cahier de doléances" and "symbol: La Marseillaise") and one question (e.g., "Did pamphlets make people support the revolution or just reflect their views?").
entry_ticket.prompt: Write two examples (one line each) of newspapers, pamphlets, symbols, or economic tools used during the French Revolution that you remember from the last lesson. Then write one quick question you still have about how these influenced public opinion.

exit_ticket.prompt: Choose one short passage used in class and: (a) name the pamphlet/newspaper or the author cited in the passage, (b) state briefly how the passage shows the print source influenced public debate, and (c) give one plausible alternative interpretation that weakens the claim that the print source caused the change.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Answer includes: (a) an identified pamphlet/newspaper or author from the passage, (b) a clear link showing influence (e.g., call to action, reported response, evidence of readers acting), and (c) a plausible counter-interpretation (e.g., reflects existing opinion, copies other sources, or overstates causation).

homework.submission_format: Printed paragraph with copied passage or uploaded photo/PDF
tasks: Select one short entry from the compiled bibliography used in class. Find (or re-read) a primary passage it cites about a pamphlet or newspaper. Copy the passage (2–4 sentences) and write a one-paragraph (6–8 sentences) explanation: two sentences summarise the passage, two sentences explain how the passage could be used as evidence that print influenced debate, and two sentences give an alternative interpretation that limits that evidence.
Bring the paragraph and the copied passage to the next class (or upload a photo/PDF).

mentor_moment.story: In 1790s France a poorly phrased handbill blamed market women for shortages; a printer rushed copies and crowds reacted before authorities could respond.
mentor_moment.takeaway: Small wording in a pamphlet can spark immediate action, so when you judge influence look closely at exactly what was printed and how people could read it.
mentor_moment.title: A printer's slip that changed a crowd

anticipated_questions: Do I have to share my exact words? (Yes — just one short example and your question.)
What if I wrote something wrong? (Write what you remember; mistakes help us learn.)
Can I pick a new example now? (Use what you wrote first.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write 3 student examples and 2 questions from entry tickets (copy exact short phrases).
teacher_script.heading: Activate prior knowledge and collect entry tickets
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Take out the quick list you just wrote. I will collect one sentence from each of you: name one example you wrote and your question. Speak loud enough for me to write a few on the board." Walk the room listening. If a student hesitates, prompt: "Is that an example of a pamphlet, a newspaper, a symbol, or an economic tool?" After 3–4 student answers, say: "Good — keep your papers. We'll use them again."

anticipated_questions: Which word makes it a claim and not a fact? (Look for verbs like 'argued', 'claimed', or 'urged'.)
What do you mean by 'concrete example'? (A named person, event, policy, or quote the pamphlet uses.)
Where do I find this passage in the packet? (Point to the page number or location in the compiled bibliography excerpt.)
teacher_script.board_action: On the board, write the passage line; underline the claim sentence, circle the concrete example name, and add the note 'audience = readers in Paris/elite'.
teacher_script.heading: Model close reading of one Chisick/Britannica passage
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "I am going to read a short passage from the Chisick citation that describes a pamphlet's claim. Listen and watch me mark the evidence." Read aloud a prepared short passage: "[Read a two-sentence excerpt attributing a claim that a pamphlet published by the Ami du Roi attacked ministerial policy and offered a concrete example — name the pamphlet's claim and the example given]." Then say: "Now watch me: I will underline the claim, circle the concrete example, and write a short note saying who the pamphlet aimed at." Demonstrate underlining the sentence that states the pamphlet's claim, circling the named example (read it aloud), and writing: 'audience = readers in Paris/elite' below. Ask: "What word shows this is a claim, not a fact?" Pause and accept answers.

anticipated_questions: Do we have to quote exactly? (Write the short phrase or paraphrase and note the line number.)
What counts as 'influenced public debate'? (Mentioned reactions, changes in speech, references by politicians, or distribution numbers.)
What is an 'alternative interpretation'? (A different reason the same passage might show, e.g., it reflected existing opinion rather than caused change.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the instructions as a checklist: 1) List 2 pieces of evidence; 2) Write 1 alternative interpretation. Leave space to add two group examples later.
teacher_script.heading: Guided group annotation of a second passage
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Now in groups of 3, each group will read a second short passage from the compiled bibliography I hand out. Your job: list two pieces of textual evidence that the pamphlet/newspaper influenced public debate and then write one plausible alternative interpretation — one sentence each. Use the evidence we modeled." Hand out the second passage (from the bibliography). Walk groups: ask each group to show their two evidence phrases and the alternative. If a group only lists claims, prompt: "Where in the passage is the link to public reaction or policy?" Circulate and note one strong example from two groups to highlight later.

anticipated_questions: Can we pick any role? (Choose one of the four listed.)
How long is the argument? (One minute per side.)
Can we use outside facts we remember? (Use the passage first; you may mention one known fact if directly relevant.)
teacher_script.board_action: List roles and a one-line prompt: 'Change outcomes or reflect opinion? — cite one evidence + one counter-interpretation.'
teacher_script.heading: Debate / role play in groups
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Now each group picks a role: publisher, royalist critic, popular reader, or historian. Spend five minutes preparing a one-minute argument answering: 'Did this pamphlet change outcomes or merely reflect opinion?' Use at least one piece of evidence from your passage and one alternative interpretation. Then I will call two groups to present short debates." Signal time: after five minutes, call two groups: one group speaks as publisher or popular reader, the other as critic or historian.
